Objectives

  • Update On Multi-modal Management Of Gastric Cancer
  • Review Landmark Trials In Gastric Cancer Management
  • Describe The Oncological Gastrectomy With Lymphadenectomy

Incidence

  • Globally, >1,000,000 cases /year
  • Fifth most frequently diagnosed cancer
  • Third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the world

Bray F, Ferlay J, Soerjomataram I, Siegel RL, Torre LA, Jemal A. Global cancer statistics 2018: GLOBOCAN estimates of incidence and mortality worldwide for

36 cancers in 185 countries. CA Cancer J Clin. 2018 Nov;68(6):394-424. doi: 10.3322/caac.21492. Epub 2018 Sep 12. Erratum in: CA Cancer J Clin. 2020

Jul;70(4):313. PMID: 30207593.

Notes

Epidemiology

Gastric cancer is less common than colorectal cancer locally, but has a higher incidence in some Eastern populations, e.g. Korea.
Globally: ~1 million cases/year; the 5th most frequently diagnosed cancer and the 3rd leading cause of cancer mortality.
Usually more common in males than females.

Risk Factors

  • H. Pylori
  • Smoking
  • Diet
  • Age
  • M >> F
  • Family History
  • Previous gastric surgery
  • MALToma with evidence of H. pylori → treatment antibiotics (H. pylori eradication — low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma regresses after eradication). 434
Notes

Risk Factors

Increasing age
Male sex
Family history / genetic predisposition
Smoking
H. pylori infection
Salt-preserved foods
Smoked/processed meats (e.g. hot dogs)
Sugary drinks
Alcohol
Previous gastric surgery (esp. prior peptic ulcer resection)
NOTE ON DIETARY RISK FACTORS
Dietary associations (salt-preserved foods, processed meats, sugary drinks, alcohol) represent correlation/risk, not necessarily direct causation.
  • Organism that carries the risk of upper GI neoplastic disease → Helicobacter pylori (commonest cause of peptic ulcer and gastric adenocarcinoma worldwide). 431 ×3
Notes

H. pylori

H. pylori is a bacterium commonly infecting the stomach; lecture prevalence ~25–30%.
Disrupts gastric mucosal protective mechanisms → predisposes to ulceration / chronic gastritis.
Persistent inflammation → impaired mucosal repair + accumulation of mutations → increased gastric cancer risk.
HIGH-YIELD PRINCIPLE
Long-standing repetitive inflammation → increased malignancy risk.
Long-standing repetitive inflammation → increased malignancy risk.

Hereditary Cancer Predisposition Syndromes

  • 3-5% of all gastric cancers are inherited cancer predisposition syndromes
  • Referral to a cancer genetics professional is recommended
Notes

Genetic Predisposition

~5% of gastric cancers are estimated to have a genetic basis.

Hereditary Diffuse Gastric Cancer

  • Autosomal dominant syndrome
  • Germline truncating mutations in tumor suppressor gene CDH1 (encoding E-cadherin) are found in 30-50% of families with HDGC
  • Prophylactic Total Gastrectomy (without D2) is recommended between 18 and 40 years
  • Screening endoscopy with multiple random biopsies every 6-12 months when prophylactic gastrectomy performed
  • Women have increased risk of breast Ca (lobular)

Pharoah PD, Guilford P, Caldas C. Incidence of gastric cancer and breast cancer in CDH1 (E-cadherin) mutation carriers from hereditary diffuse gastric cancer families.

Gastroenterology 2001;121:1348-1353.

Notes

Hereditary Diffuse Gastric Cancer (HDGC)

MOST IMPORTANT INHERITED GASTRIC CANCER SYNDROME — KNOW THIS
Autosomal dominant
Mutation in CDH1 → encodes E-cadherin, a cell-adhesion protein
Associated with diffuse-type gastric cancer
Lifetime gastric cancer risk is very high — almost 100%
Female carriers also have markedly increased risk of lobular breast cancer
MANAGEMENT OF CDH1 CARRIERS
Patients may be offered prophylactic total gastrectomy, potentially from young adulthood (~18 years), or otherwise require extensive lifelong gastric surveillance. Once a mutation is identified, relatives should be offered genetic testing/counselling.

Other Genetic Syndromes

SyndromeMechanismAssociation
Lynch syndromeDNA mismatch-repair pathway abnormalityColorectal, endometrial & intestinal-type gastric cancer
FAPAPC pathwayCan also predispose to gastric cancer
HDGC (CDH1)E-cadherin loss of functionDiffuse-type gastric cancer + lobular breast cancer
Lecture focus for examination/management = HDGC/CDH1.
  • Germline truncating mutations in tumor suppressor gene CDH1 (encoding

E-cadherin) are found in 30-50% of families with HDGC

  • Diffuse type Gastric Cancer
The most important inherited gastric cancer syndrome — know this. Autosomal dominant; germline truncating mutations in the tumour-suppressor gene CDH1 (encodes E-cadherin, a cell-adhesion protein) — found in 30–50% of HDGC families → diffuse-type gastric cancer.

Lynch Syndrome

  • Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer
  • Colorectal, endometrial, and gastric cancers
  • Germline mutations in any of the four DNA mismatch repair genes( MLH1, MSH2,

MSH6, and PMS2)

  • Intestinal type Gastric Cancer
  • Extended EGD may be considered as screening strategy

Other Syndromes

  • Familial Adnomatous Polyposis
    • APC gene mutations
    • 1-2% lifetime risk for GC
  • Peutz Jeghers Syndrome
    • STK11 tumor suppressor gene mutations
    • 29% lifetime risk for GC
    • Screening may be considered beginning in the late teens
    • Repeat every 2-3 years
  • Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome
    • SMAD4 or BMPR1A mutations
    • 21% lifetime risk for GC mainly in SMAD4 mutation carriers
    • Screen early mid-teens
  • Other Syndromes:
    • Ataxia-telangiectasis, Bloom Syndrome, Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer Syndrome, Li-Fraumeni Syndrome, Cowden syndrome and Others

Classifications

  • Number of different classifications:
    • Lauren Classification
      • Intestinal, Diffuse, Mixed
    • WHO Classification
      • Papillary, Tubular, Mucinous, Poorly cohesive, Signet Ring
    • Borrmann’s classification of AGC
      • Polypoid, Fungating, Ulcerative, Diffusely Infiltrating
Kim G.H. (2018) Advanced Gastric Cancers. In: Chun H., Yang SK., Choi MG. (eds) ClinicalBorrmann’s classification

Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. Springer, Singapore. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-10-4995-8_12

Linitis Plastica

  • Macroscopic thickening of gastric wall, often involving entire stomach
  • No distinct mass
  • Submucosal infiltration
  • Poorly distensible stomach
  • Difficult to obtain tissue diagnosis
  • Total gastrectomy and lymphadenectomy
  • Aggressive biology (peritoneal mets)
Notes

Classification

Lauren Classification

The most commonly emphasized classification — clinically relevant because different tumor types may have different biology/management.

TypeKey Association
Intestinal typeAssociated with Lynch syndrome
Diffuse typeAssociated with HDGC / CDH1 mutation
Mixed typeFeatures of both
Borrmann ClassificationMore advanced molecular/genetic classifications exist but were beyond lecture scope.
Gross morphological classification — tumors may appear:
• Fungating
• Ulcerative
• Diffuse infiltrative
• Polypoid
Linitis Plastica
WARNING — CAN BE MISSED ON BIOPSY
Important form of diffuse infiltrative gastric cancer
Tumor infiltrates the submucosa/wall → stomach becomes thick, rigid, poorly distensible
On endoscopy, stomach does not inflate normally with air
Superficial mucosal biopsy may be false-negative — malignant tissue is predominantly deeper/submucosal
Aggressive biology; often diagnosed at an advanced stage
DIAGNOSIS WHEN LINITIS PLASTICA SUSPECTED
EUS-guided biopsy — visualizes gastric wall layers, allows targeted deep biopsy
Tunnel biopsy — repeated biopsies from the same site to progressively reach submucosa
Suspected linitis plastica → EUS-guided biopsy (targets the deep layers) or tunnel biopsy (repeated biopsies at the same site to reach the submucosa).

Presentation

  • Early disease can be asymptomatic
  • Symptoms of indigestion, Nausea and vomiting, Dysphagia,

Postprandial fullness, loss of appetite, melena, hematemesis, weight loss

  • Late Complications including peritoneal/pleural effusions, gastric outlet obstruction, bleeding, jaundice, cachexia, ….
  • 68-year-old, recurrent non-bilious vomiting of undigested food, 13 kg weight loss, cachectic and pale → obstructed gastric outlet (from gastric cancer). 439 ×2
Notes

Clinical Presentation

Early Disease

Most patients are asymptomatic or have vague abdominal pain/dyspeptic symptoms.
Stomach has a large capacity → tumors may become large before producing obstruction.
Tumors at narrow regions cause symptoms earlier: gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) and pylorus.
Tumors in the gastric body may grow considerably before detection.
Notes

Progressive / Late Disease

FindingSignificance
ObstructionDistension, vomiting; succussion splash with gastric outlet obstruction
BleedingMay present with anemia or overt GI bleeding
PerforationSurgical emergency
Virchow nodeLeft supraclavicular lymphadenopathy — metastatic spread
Sister Mary Joseph nodulePeriumbilical metastatic deposit
Alarm Features → Endoscopy
REFER FOR ENDOSCOPY IF:
Dysphagia · Weight loss · Significant anemia · Symptoms failing to respond to treatment
Alarm features → endoscopy: dysphagia · weight loss · significant anaemia · symptoms failing to respond to treatment.

Workup and Staging

  • Patient Medical History and Physical Examination
  • CBC and comprehensive chemistry profile
  • Upper GI endoscopy and biopsy (Siewert tumor type should be included if EGJ adenocarcinoma)
  • EUS
  • CT Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis
  • FDG-PET/CT if clinically indicated
  • Diagnostic Laparoscopy
  • Gastric adenocarcinoma on biopsy → most appropriate next step → CT scan (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging; EUS/laparoscopy follow). 433
Notes

Diagnosis & Initial Workup

StepDetails
HistoryPresenting symptoms, risk factors, family history/genetic predisposition
Physical examAbdominal masses, evidence of metastatic disease
LabsCBC, liver function tests, renal function, nutritional profile
EndoscopyBiopsy of suspicious ulcer/mass for histologic confirmation; report should describe location and relationship to GEJ
REMEMBER
There is no specific tumor marker that reliably diagnoses gastric cancer.
There is no specific tumour marker that reliably diagnoses gastric cancer.
Notes

Staging

Goal: define local tumor characteristics/depth and detect distant metastasis.

Notes

Main Staging Modalities

CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (CT-CAP)
Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)
± Diagnostic/staging laparoscopy

GEJ Tumors — Siewert Classification

For tumors around the gastroesophageal junction, Siewert I, II, III classify whether the tumor is predominantly esophageal side, at the GE junction, or gastric side.

Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS)

Defines depth of tumor invasion (T stage) by visualizing individual gastric wall layers.
Particularly useful for differentiating early T1 disease from deeper T2 disease.
If CT already shows clearly advanced transmural disease, EUS may add little.
KEY THRESHOLD — T1B
T1b = invasion into submucosa. Lecture approach: T1b or deeper disease carries significant risk of occult peritoneal metastasis → consider staging laparoscopy.
T1b (submucosal invasion) or deeper → significant risk of occult peritoneal metastasis → staging laparoscopy.

EUS

  • EUS Essential for small ?early lesions (T1 and T2)
  • Endoscopic resection needed to differentiate between T1a and T1b
  • Operator dependent
  • T-stage accuracy (60-90%)
  • N-stage accuracy (50-80%)
Notes

Peritoneal Metastasis & Staging Laparoscopy

Peritoneum = major metastatic site for gastric cancer.
Small peritoneal deposits can be missed on CT → direct laparoscopic assessment may detect otherwise occult metastases.
DURING DIAGNOSTIC LAPAROSCOPY
Inspect abdominal cavity for peritoneal deposits
If no visible disease → perform peritoneal lavage/washings
Saline placed into abdominal quadrants → aspirated → sent for cytology for malignant cells
PRACTICAL POINT
Because cytology requires processing time, staging laparoscopy should generally be completed as a staging procedure rather than immediately proceeding to definitive gastrectomy before results are known.

After history, examination, labs, imaging, EUS ± laparoscopy → estimate final clinical TNM stage.

Diagnostic Laparoscopy

  • ≥T1b
  • Cytology testing of peritoneal fluid
  • Prior to chemotherapy
  • For patient undergoing R0 resection or chemoradiation
  • Can avoid unnecessary laparotomy

American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM Staging Classification for Carcinoma of the Stomach (8th ed., 2017) — Table 1. Definitions for T, N, M

TisCarcinoma in situ: intraepithelial tumor without invasion of the lamina propria, high-grade dysplasia
T1Tumor invades the lamina propria, muscularis mucosae, or submucosa

T4Tumor invades the serosa (visceral peritoneum) or adjacent structures,*
T4aTumor invades the serosa (visceral peritoneum)
T4bTumor invades adjacent structures/organs
NRegional Lymph Nodes
NXRegional lymph node(s) cannot be assessed
N0No regional lymph node metastasis
N1Metastasis in one or two regional lymph nodes
N2Metastasis in three to six regional lymph nodes
N3Metastasis in seven or more regional lymph nodes
N3aMetastasis in seven to 15 regional lymph nodes
N3bMetastasis in 16 or more regional lymph nodes

GHistologic Grade
GXGrade cannot be assessed
G1Well differentiated

*A tumor may penetrate the muscularis propria with extension into the gastrocolic or gastrohepatic ligaments, or into the greater or lesser omentum, without perforation of the visceral peritoneum covering these structures. In this case, the tumor is classified as T3. If there is perforation of the visceral peritoneum covering the gastric ligaments or the omentum, the tumor should be classified as T4.

**The adjacent structures of the stomach include the spleen, transverse colon, liver, diaphragm, pancreas, abdominal wall, adrenal gland, kidney, small intestine, and retroperitoneum.

***Intramural extension to the duodenum or esophagus is not considered invasion of an adjacent structure, but is classified using the depth of the greatest invasion in any of these sites.

Treatment

  • Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Discussion
  • Combined Modality Therapy
    • Surgery
    • Chemotherapy
    • Chemoradiation
    • Targeted therapies
Notes

Treatment

Modalities: endoscopic resection, surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted/biologic therapies where appropriate.

StageApproach
Tis / T1a (very early, <2 cm, no metastasis)May be amenable to endoscopic resection
T1bGenerally requires surgical resection rather than endoscopic treatment
T2 or higherNeoadjuvant chemotherapy → surgery → adjuvant chemotherapy
Exact chemotherapy protocols were not required for this lecture; know the treatment modality/sequence.

Total Gastrectomy

Subtotal Gastrectomy

Regional Lymphatics

  • Gastric resection should include the regional lymphatics
    • perigastric lymph nodes (D1) and those along the named vessels of the celiac axis (D2), with a goal of examining at least 16 or greater lymph nodes
  • Definition of D1 and D2 lymph node dissections
    • D1 dissection entails gastrectomy and the resection of both the greater and lesser omenta (which would include the lymph nodes along right and left cardiac, lesser and greater curvature, suprapyloric along the right gastric artery, and infrapyloric area)
    • D2 dissection is a D1 plus all the nodes along the left gastric artery, common hepatic artery, celiac artery, and splenic artery.
Notes

Surgery

Tumor LocationProcedure
Proximal tumorTotal gastrectomy
Distal tumorSubtotal / distal gastrectomy
Both are usually combined with D2 lymphadenectomy. D2 Lymphadenectomy
• D1 nodes: perigastric lymph-node stations immediately around the stomach (stations 1–7).
• D2: extends dissection to second-order nodes along branches of the celiac trunk.
• Standard oncologic gastrectomy = gastrectomy + D2 lymphadenectomy.
• Reconstruction commonly performed using a Roux-en-Y configuration.

Treatment

  • Initial workup enables patients to be classified as:
    • Localized cancer (stages cTis or cT1a)
    • Locoregional cancer (stages cT1b-cT4a; cM0)
    • Metastatic Cancer (stage cT4b; cM1)
  • Additional evaluation of health status and resectability divides patients into:
  • Medically fit patients with potentially resectable disease
  • Medically fit patient with unresectable disease
  • Non-surgical candidates (medically unable or decline surgery)
  • Gastric Cancer is unresectable when:
    • Peritoneal involvement (including positive cytology)
    • Distant metastases
    • Locally advanced disease (N3 or N4 lymph nodes, invasion of major vascular structures excluding splenic vessels)
Unresectable: peritoneal involvement (including positive cytology), distant metastases, locally advanced disease (N3/N4 nodes, invasion of major vascular structures excluding splenic vessels).

East vs West guidelines

Algorithm of standard treatments. The T/N/M and Stage are used in conjunction with the Japanese Classification of Gastric Carcinoma 15th edition and TNM classification 8th edition

StagePatientPrimary treatmentNext
cTis or cT1a→ Non-surgical candidate→ ER→ Endoscopic surveillance
cTis or cT1a→ Medically fit→ ER or Surgery→ ER → Endoscopic surveillance · Surgery → Surgical Outcomes for Patients Who Have Not Received Preoperative Therapy (see GAST-4)

Early Gastric Cancer

  • T1 lesion, regardless of nodal status
  • Uncommon and often discovered incidentally
  • T1a (mucosa) ~5% risk of LN mets
  • T1b (submucosa) ~15-20% risk of LN mets
  • EMR/ESD criteria:
    • Well/mod diff
    • Non-ulcerated
    • T1a (mucosa)
    • ≤2cm
StagePatientPrimary treatmentNext
cTis or cT1a→ Non-surgical candidate→ ER→ Endoscopic surveillance
cTis or cT1a→ Medically fit→ ER or Surgery→ ER → Endoscopic surveillance · Surgery → Surgical Outcomes for Patients Who Have Not Received Preoperative Therapy (see GAST-4)
EMR/ESD criteria: well/moderately differentiated · non-ulcerated · T1a (mucosa) · ≤ 2 cm.

Endoscopic Resection

Surveillance Post R0 resection

p stage I (T1a,T1b, N0–1 treated by surgical resection or T1a treated by ER) →

  • H&P every 3–6 months for 1–2 years, every 6–12 months for 3–5 years, and annually thereafter
  • CBC and chemistry profile as clinically indicated
  • For patients treated by ER, EGD every 6 months for 1 year, then annually for up to 5 years
    • Thereafter, as needed based on symptoms and/or radiographic findings
  • For patients treated by surgical resection, EGD as clinically indicated
  • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with oral and IV contrast as clinically indicated
  • Monitor for nutritional deficiency (eg, B12 and iron) in surgically resected patients (especially after total gastrectomy) and treat as indicated

Landmark Trials in Gastric Cancer

The INT-0116 Trial (Macdonald Trial)

  • N=556 gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma Stage IB or greater (non-metastatic)
  • R0 resection Surgery vs. Surgery plus adjuvant ChemoRT (5-FU)
  • **85% of patients were node positive

Role of Radiotherapy

Not routinely required after adequate surgery; mainly considered with suboptimal oncologic resection, especially:

Positive surgical margins
Inadequate lymph-node harvest (lecture: approximately <15–16 nodes is inadequate for reliable staging) Otherwise → proceed with adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery.

Perioperative Chemotherapy

  • Survival benefit of perioperative chemotherapy (chemo then surgery then chemo) was first demonstrated in the landmark phase III MAGIC trial

Cunningham D, Allum WH, Stenning SP, et al. Perioperative chemotherapy versus surgery alone for resectable gastroesophageal cancer. N Engl J Med 2006;355:11-20.

  • This was the gold standard until FLOT4 trial significantly higher OS (50 months vs 35 months; HR = 0.77; 95% Ci, 0.63-0.94)

MAGIC Trial

  • Surgery vs. Peri-operative chemotherapy+Surgery

ARTIST Trial

  • The results of the phase III ARTIST trial:
    • postoperative chemoradiation did not significantly reduce recurrence rates after D2 lymph node dissection in patients with curatively resected gastric cancer compared to postoperative chemotherapy.
    • Improved DFS in sub-group analysis of node-positive patients who received chemoRT
  • However, the phase III ARTIST II trial:
    • no survival benefit for postoperative chemoradiation in patients with node-positive, D2-resected gastric cancer (3-year DFS of 78% vs. 73% for postoperative chemotherapy and postoperative chemoradiation, respectively;

P = .667).

Lee J, Lim do H, Kim S, et al. Phase III trial comparing capecitabine plus cisplatin versus capecitabine plus cisplatin with concurrent capecitabine radiotherapy in completely resected gastric cancer with D2 lymph node dissection: the ARTIST trial. J Clin Oncol 2012;30:268-273

Treatment

  • Perioperative chemotherapy for all non-metastatic ≥ cT2 or ≥ N1
  • D2 lymph node dissection is recommended for all

≥cT2 or ≥N1

(NCCN recommended but not required as long as >15 LNs are examined)

  • Chemoradiation is recommended for patients who received less than a D2 lymph node dissection

Follow-up

p stage II/III or yp stage I–III (treated with neoadjuvant ± adjuvant therapy) →

  • H&P every 3–6 months for 1–2 years, every 6–12 months for 3–5 years, and annually thereafter
  • CBC and chemistry profile as clinically indicated
  • For patients who had partial or subtotal gastrectomy, EGD as clinically indicated
  • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with oral and IV contrast (preferred) every 6–12 months for first 2 years, then annually up to 5 years and/or can consider FDG-PET/CT as clinically indicated
  • Monitor for nutritional deficiency (eg, B12 and iron) in surgically resected patients (especially after total gastrectomy) and treat as indicated

Unresectable locally advanced, Locally recurrent or metastatic disease

PerformanceTestingTreatment
Karnofsky performance score ≥60% or ECOG performance score ≤2→ Perform HER2, PD-L1, MSI by PCR/MMR by IHC testing (if not done previously) if metastatic adenocarcinoma is documented or suspected · *If sufficient tissue is available after the above testing has been completed, NGS may be considered*→ Chemoradiation (only if locally unresectable and not previously received) or Systemic therapy or Best supportive care
Karnofsky performance score <60% or ECOG performance score ≥3→ Best supportive care

Complicated Gastric Cancer

  • Adjacent Organ Involvement
    • Pre-op treatment (perioperative chemotherapy)
    • Diagnostic Laparoscopy
    • En-bloc resection
Notes

Metastatic Gastric Cancer

PROGNOSIS AND APPROACH
Most metastatic gastric cancers → palliative rather than curative treatment.
Extensive metastasectomy for solid-organ metastatic disease is generally not standard.
Peritoneal metastases also generally imply palliative disease.
Some centers may offer HIPEC in selected patients with peritoneal disease, but this is not standard therapy.

Summary

  • Gastric cancer is often diagnosed at advanced stages
  • Risk factors for gastric cancer include H. pylori infection, smoking, and high salt intake
  • Some gastric cancers are associated with inherited gastric cancer predisposition syndromes.
  • multidisciplinary team management as essential for the management of patients with gastric cancer.
  • Best supportive care is an integral part of treatment, especially in patients with locally advanced or metastatic disease.

Gastric Carcinoma
1. Epidemiology
  • 26,000 new cases annually in the U.S.
  • Incidence has dropped by two-thirds in the last 40 years (due to declining H.

pylori infection).

  • High-risk regions: South Korea (41.8 per 100,000).
  • More common in men (2:1 ratio) and in patients aged 40–60 (mean age 63).
Risk Factors
  • H. pylori infection (3.6- to 18-fold increased risk).
  • Chronic atrophic gastritis (precursor to cancer).
  • Dietary factors (low vegetable/fruit intake, high salt, starch, smoked foods).
  • Smoking.
2. Pathology & Classification
Histology
  • 95% of gastric cancers are adenocarcinomas.
  • Two major histologic types:
  • Intestinal type → Better prognosis, glandular differentiation.
  • Diffuse type → Poorly differentiated, infiltrative, worse prognosis.
  • Signet ring cell carcinoma → More common in younger patients and women.
Morphologic Types

1. Ulcerating carcinoma (25%) → Deep, penetrates all layers.

2. Polypoid carcinoma (25%) → Large, bulky, late metastasis.

3. Superficial spreading carcinoma (15%) → Limited to mucosa/submucosa,

  • best prognosis.

4. Linitis plastica (10%) → Infiltrative growth, rigid stomach, poor prognosis.

5. Advanced carcinoma (35%) → Large tumors extending beyond stomach.

Common Locations:
  • Antrum (40%).
  • Body/Fundus (30%).
  • Cardia (25%).
  • Entire stomach (5%).
Spread:
  • Direct invasion → Pancreas, liver, colon.
  • Lymphatic metastases.
  • Peritoneal dissemination → Krukenberg tumors (ovary), Blumer shelf (rectum).
  • Virchow node (left supraclavicular lymph node).

Staging is crucial (Table 25-3 outlines TNM staging).

3. Clinical Presentation
Early symptoms are non-specific:
  • Postprandial fullness.
  • Mild dyspepsia.
  • Anorexia (especially for meat).
  • Weight loss (most common, ~6 kg).
Advanced symptoms:
  • Epigastric mass (~25% cases).
  • GI bleeding (melena, hematemesis, occult blood).
  • Obstruction (vomiting, dysphagia if cardia is involved).
  • Signs of metastasis:
  • Virchow node (supraclavicular).
  • Blumer shelf (rectal peritoneal deposits).
  • Krukenberg tumors (ovarian involvement).
4. Diagnosis
A. Laboratory Findings
  • Iron deficiency anemia (40%).
  • Elevated carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) (65%) → May indicate metastases.
  • HER2 overexpression testing → Guides therapy.
B. Imaging
  • Upper endoscopy with biopsy (Gold Standard) → At least 6 biopsies needed.
  • CT/PET/MRI for staging & metastasis detection.
  • Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) → Determines depth of invasion & lymph node

involvement.

  • Laparoscopy → Used in cases where metastases are suspected but not

confirmed on imaging.

C. Barium X-ray (rarely used)
  • Can detect gastric ulcers and mass lesions but false negatives in 20% of cases.
5. Treatment
  • Surgical resection is the only curative option.
  • Preoperative chemotherapy (neoadjuvant) recommended for locally

advanced cases.

A. Surgical Options
1. Distal gastrectomy (For tumors in the antrum)
  • Removes tumor, omentum, duodenum, regional lymph nodes.
  • Reconstruction: Billroth I or II (Roux-en-Y is preferred).
2. Total gastrectomy (For proximal tumors/linitis plastica)
  • Requires splenectomy & Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy.
  • Frozen section at margins to ensure complete resection.
Palliative Surgery:
  • Used for unresectable tumors causing obstruction.
  • Gastrojejunostomy may be done instead of resection.
6. Chemotherapy & Targeted Therapy
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy:
  • FLOT regimen (5-FU, Leucovorin, Oxaliplatin, Docetaxel).
  • Improves survival and reduces tumor size before surgery.
Adjuvant chemotherapy:
  • Used post-surgery for node-positive disease.
Targeted Therapy:
  • Trastuzumab (HER2-positive tumors).
  • Pembrolizumab (PD-L1 inhibitors for advanced disease).

Palliative chemotherapy for metastatic disease improves survival but is not curative.

7. Prognosis & Survival Rates
  • 5-year survival (U.S.): ~31%.
  • Early gastric cancer (confined to mucosa/submucosa): 90% survival.
  • Advanced gastric cancer (lymph node/metastasis present): <20% survival.
  • In Japan (due to screening programs), early gastric cancer survival is much

higher (~70%).

Death usually results from:
  • Tumor metastasis to liver, lungs, brain, bones.
  • Gastric obstruction leading to malnutrition.
Gastric Leiomyomas & Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs)
1. Overview

Leiomyomas: Benign submucosal growths, usually asymptomatic, may cause bleeding.

Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs):

  • Previously classified as leiomyosarcomas.
  • Arise from interstitial cells of Cajal (pacemaker cells of the GI tract).
  • Most common mesenchymal tumors of the GI tract.
  • Can be malignant depending on size & mitotic index.
  • Locations: Most frequently in the proximal stomach, but also found in intestines, gallbladder, urinary bladder.
2. Clinical Presentation

Most are asymptomatic and found incidentally.

When symptomatic:

  • GI bleeding (occult or overt).
  • Epigastric pain.
  • Early satiety or bloating due to mass effect.
  • Weight loss (if malignant).
  • Perforation (rare) → Severe pain & peritonitis.
Spread:
  • Direct invasion or hematogenous spread (common sites: liver, peritoneum,

omentum).

  • Lymphatic spread is uncommon (unlike adenocarcinomas).
3. Diagnosis
  • Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) + fine-needle aspiration (FNA) (higher diagnostic

yield than endoscopic biopsy).

  • CT scan or MRI → Determines tumor size, local invasion, metastases.
  • Immunohistochemistry:
  • c-KIT (CD117) → Key diagnostic marker (95% of GISTs).
  • DOG-1, PDGFRA mutations.
Prognostic factors:
  • Tumor size (>5 cm = high risk).
  • Mitotic index (>10 mitoses per high-power field = high risk).
  • Tumor location (GISTs outside stomach tend to be more aggressive).
4. Treatment
  • GISTs ≥2 cm: Resection is recommended (even if asymptomatic).
  • Small (<2 cm), asymptomatic gastric GISTs:
  • Can be observed with periodic imaging.

✔ Leiomyomas: No intervention unless symptomatic.

A. Surgical Management
  • Wedge or segmental resection (without wide margins, unlike

adenocarcinomas).

  • More extensive resections if metastatic disease (peritoneum, liver).
  • Lymph node dissection NOT required (low risk of lymphatic spread).
B. Targeted Therapy
  • c-KIT and PDGFRA mutations → Respond to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs).
  • Imatinib (Gleevec):
  • Used for unresectable, metastatic, or high-risk tumors.
  • Given as neoadjuvant therapy to shrink tumors before surgery.
  • Adjuvant therapy after surgery for high-risk tumors (reduces recurrence).
  • Sunitinib: Second-line for imatinib-resistant GISTs.
5. Prognosis & Follow-up
  • Good prognosis if localized and resected.
  • Poor prognosis if large (>10 cm) or high mitotic index.
  • Follow-up imaging required (to detect recurrence/metastasis).
Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) Syndrome
1. Overview
  • Also called Wilkie's Syndrome.
  • Rare cause of duodenal obstruction due to compression of the third portion

of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and the aorta.

  • Commonly associated with rapid weight loss → loss of mesenteric fat reduces

the aortomesenteric angle, leading to duodenal entrapment.

  • At-risk populations:
  • Patients with severe burns, trauma, or prolonged immobilization (e.g., body

casts).

  • Anorexia nervosa or malnutrition.
  • Patients undergoing bariatric surgery or experiencing chronic weight loss.
  • Spinal cord injuries or congenital conditions with abnormal SMA anatomy.
2. Pathophysiology
Normal anatomy:
  • SMA leaves the aorta at a 50–60° angle.
  • Aortomesenteric distance = 10–20 mm.
SMA syndrome:
  • Aortomesenteric angle narrows to <25°.
  • Aortomesenteric distance shrinks to <8 mm.
  • Duodenum gets compressed, leading to intermittent or chronic obstruction.
3. Clinical Presentation
Symptoms:
  • Postprandial bloating & crampy epigastric pain.
  • Early satiety & weight loss.
  • Nausea & vomiting (bilious, non-bloody).
  • Symptoms improve in the prone or knee-chest position.
  • Malnutrition & electrolyte imbalances in chronic cases.
4. Diagnosis
Imaging Studies:
  • Upper GI series (fluoroscopy):
  • Dilatation of the proximal duodenum.
  • Abrupt "cut-off" at the third portion.
  • Relief in the knee-chest position.
  • CT angiography with contrast:
  • Confirms narrowing of aortomesenteric angle (<25°).
  • Measures reduced aortomesenteric distance (<8 mm).
  • Upper endoscopy: Rules out other causes (e.g., malignancy, peptic ulcer disease).
5. Differential Diagnosis
Scleroderma:
  • Hypomotility & dilated duodenum without significant peristalsis.
  • Usually associated with esophageal dysphagia.
Malrotation with congenital bands:
  • Similar obstruction but congenital in origin.
  • Surgical correction required.
6. Treatment
A. Conservative Management (First-Line)

Indications: Mild to moderate symptoms without severe malnutrition.

Nutritional therapy:

  • High-calorie, small frequent meals.
  • Liquid or enteral feeding (nasogastric/nasoduodenal tube if needed).
  • Parenteral nutrition for severe malnutrition.
  • Postural changes:
  • Prone or left lateral decubitus positioning after meals.
  • Knee-chest position to relieve compression. Fluid & electrolyte management if dehydration is present.
B. Surgical Management (Severe/Refractory Cases)
Indications:
  • Persistent vomiting & weight loss despite conservative treatment.
  • Complete duodenal obstruction.
Surgical options:
  • Strong’s procedure (ligament of Treitz release): Mobilizes the duodenum to

relieve compression.

  • Duodenojejunostomy (bypass procedure): Creates an anastomosis between the duodenum & jejunum.
  • Gastrojejunostomy (less commonly performed).
7. Prognosis & Follow-up
  • Excellent prognosis with early intervention.
  • Most cases improve with nutritional therapy & postural changes.
  • Surgical success rate >90% if needed.
  • Long-term follow-up: Nutritional counseling to prevent recurrence.
